title: Heaps: insert and delete, plus BST practice
overview: This module introduces the binary heap: a complete binary tree stored in a plain array, where every parent is bigger (max heap) or smaller (min heap) than its children. You learn how to insert by bubbling a value up and how to delete the root by moving the last value to the top and pushing it down. The practice problems apply BST ideas (in-order is sorted, the BST rule lets you skip branches) and a simple top-two scan.

concepts.explain: A heap is a complete tree, so it fits in an array with no gaps. For index `i`, the children are at `2*i + 1` and `2*i + 2`, and the parent is at `(i - 1) / 2`.
In a max heap every parent is at least as big as its children, so the largest value sits at index 0. A min heap is the mirror: the smallest value is at the top.

concepts.term: Insert = push back, then bubble up
concepts.explain: Add the value at the end of the array, then keep swapping it with its parent while it beats the parent. It stops at the root or when the parent is already better.

concepts.term: Delete root = move last to top, then push down
concepts.explain: Copy the last element into index 0 and remove the last slot. Then swap the top with its better child (bigger for max heap, smaller for min heap) until neither child beats it.
A complete tree with n nodes has height about log2(n), and bubbling up or down moves one level per swap, so both operations are O(log n).
Several problems here rely on it: the closest pair of values in a BST is always adjacent in in-order, and relinking nodes in in-order gives an increasing chain.

files.title: Insert into a max heap
files.what: Reads an array that is already a max heap, adds one new value and bubbles it up to its correct place, then prints the array.
steps: Read `n` and the heap into `v`, then read `val` and `push_back` it.
`cur_idx` starts at the last index, where the new value sits.
Compute `par_idx = (cur_idx - 1) / 2`. If `v[cur_idx] > v[par_idx]`, swap them and move `cur_idx` up to the parent.
Stop when the value is not bigger than its parent, or when it reaches index 0.
Print the array: it is still a valid max heap.
files.complexity: Time O(log n) · Space O(1) extra
files.input_note: n, then a valid max heap of n values in array order, then the value to insert.
files.output_note: `60 40 55 10 30 20 50`: 55 started at index 6, beat its parent 50 at index 2 and swapped, then stopped under 60 because 55 < 60.
files.watch_out: The input array must already be a heap; the program does not build one from arbitrary values.

check.q: If you inserted 70 instead of 55, what would the array become?

files.title: Insert into a min heap
files.what: The mirror of the max heap insert: the new value bubbles up while it is smaller than its parent.
steps: Read the existing min heap and the new value, then append the value.
While `cur_idx != 0`, compare with the parent at `(cur_idx - 1) / 2`.
Swap when `v[cur_idx] < v[par_idx]`; otherwise stop.
Print the array.
files.complexity: Time O(log n) · Space O(1) extra
files.input_note: n, then a valid min heap, then the value to insert.
files.output_note: `5 20 10 40 50 60 30`: 5 swapped with 30 (index 2), then with 10 (index 0), and is now the smallest value at the top.

check.q: What is the only change from the max heap version?
check.a: The comparison: `<` instead of `>` when deciding to swap with the parent.

files.title: Delete the root of a max heap
files.what: Builds a max heap by inserting values one by one, prints it, then removes the root by moving the last value up and pushing it down.
steps: `heap_input` reads `n` values and calls `insert_heap` for each, so the vector is a max heap after every step.
`delete_heap` copies `v.back()` into `v[0]` and pops the last element.
In a loop it reads the child values; a missing child counts as `INT_MIN` so it never wins.
If the left child is the bigger child and beats the current value, swap with it and move down; same for the right child.
When neither child is bigger, the heap is fixed and the function returns.
The commented-out `delete_heap_mine` stopped as soon as the right child was missing, which can leave a left child bigger than its parent. The final version fixes that with the `INT_MIN` trick.
files.complexity: Time O(n log n) to build, O(log n) to delete · Space O(n)
files.input_note: n, then n values in any order.
files.output_note: There is no output: the file does not compile (see below). With the fix it prints the heap `60 40 50 10 30 20`; the delete then changes it to `50 40 20 10 30`.
files.watch_out: `delete_heap` is missing its closing `}`, so the compiler sees `main` inside it and fails with `a function-definition is not allowed here`. Fix: add `}` before `int main()`. Also `main` never prints after deleting; add `print_heap(v);` after `delete_heap(v);` to see the result.

check.q: Why swap with the bigger child and not just any child that beats the parent?
check.a: The bigger child becomes the new parent of the other child, so it must be at least as big as that child, or the heap rule breaks.

files.title: Delete the root of a min heap
files.what: The min heap version of root deletion: the moved value is pushed down towards the smaller child, and missing children count as `INT_MAX`.
steps: `insert_heap` bubbles up while the value is smaller than its parent.
`delete_heap` moves the last value to index 0 and pops the back.
Missing children are treated as `INT_MAX`, so they never look smaller.
Swap with the smaller child while it is smaller than the current value; stop otherwise.
files.complexity: Time O(n log n) to build, O(log n) to delete · Space O(n)
files.input_note: n, then n values in any order.
files.output_note: There is no output: the same missing brace stops it compiling. With the fix it prints `10 30 20 50 40 60`, and the delete leaves `20 30 60 50 40`.
files.watch_out: The same bug as the max heap file: `delete_heap` has no closing `}`, so compilation fails. Add `}` before `int main()`, and add `print_heap(v);` after the delete to see the result.

check.q: Why use `INT_MAX` for a missing child in a min heap?
check.a: The code looks for a child smaller than the current value; `INT_MAX` is never smaller, so a missing child is never chosen.

files.title: Code360: insert into a BST

problem.name: Code360 - Insert Into A Binary Search Tree

files.what: A short recursive BST insert that returns the (possibly new) root of each subtree.
steps: If `root` is `NULL`, the empty spot has been found: return a new node holding `val`.
If `val` is smaller, set `root->left` to the result of inserting into the left subtree.
Otherwise set `root->right` to the result of inserting into the right subtree.
Return `root` so the parent keeps pointing to the same node.
files.input_note: n, then n values inserted one by one into an empty BST.
files.output_note: After each insert the in-order walk is still sorted (`3 8`, `3 8 10`, ... `1 3 6 8 10 14`), which shows every value went to the right place. The first value, 8, stays the root.

check.q: Why does this version not need `Node* &root`?
check.a: It returns the new subtree root and the caller stores it in `root->left` or `root->right`, so no reference is needed.

files.title: LeetCode 938: range sum of BST
files.what: Adds up all values between `low` and `high`, using the BST rule to skip subtrees that cannot contain any value in range.
steps: An empty tree contributes 0.
If the node is below `low`, its whole left subtree is too small, so only search the right.
If the node is above `high`, only search the left.
Otherwise the node is in range: add its value plus the sums from both sides.
files.complexity: Time O(n) worst case, often much less · Space O(h)
files.input_note: Tree values in level order, -1 for a missing child (tree `[10,5,15,3,7,null,18]`), then `low high` (LeetCode example 1).
files.output_note: `rangeSumBST = 32`, as LeetCode expects: 7 + 10 + 15. Node 3 is never visited, because 5 is below `low` and the search goes only to its right.

check.q: With `low = 7` and the node 5, why can the left subtree of 5 be skipped?
check.a: Everything to the left of 5 is smaller than 5, so it is also below 7.

files.title: LeetCode 530: minimum absolute difference in BST

problem.name: LeetCode 530 - Minimum Absolute Difference in BST

files.what: Walks the BST in order (sorted order) and compares each value with the one just before it; the smallest gap is the answer.
steps: `prev` remembers the last node visited and `min_diff` starts at `INT_MAX`.
`inorderTraversal` goes left first, then handles the current node, then goes right.
When `prev` exists, update `min_diff` with `node->val - prev->val`.
Set `prev = node` and continue; return `min_diff` at the end.
files.input_note: Tree values in level order, -1 for a missing child (tree `[4,2,6,1,3]`, the LeetCode example).
files.output_note: `getMinimumDifference = 1`, as LeetCode expects. The in-order walk visits 1 2 3 4 6, and neighbouring values such as 1 and 2 differ by 1.

check.q: Why is it enough to compare only neighbours in in-order?
check.a: In-order gives sorted values, and in a sorted list the smallest gap is always between two adjacent values.

files.title: LeetCode 897: increasing order search tree
files.what: Relinks the BST nodes, in in-order, into a chain where every node has only a right child.
steps: A dummy node `start` (value 999) sits before the chain; `current` points to the last node of the chain.
`inorder` visits the left subtree first.
For the current node it clears `node->left`, attaches the node as `current->right`, and moves `current` to it.
Then it visits the right subtree; `current` is passed by reference so every call extends the same chain.
`increasingBST` returns `start->right`, the first real node.
files.input_note: Tree values in level order, -1 for a missing child (tree `[5,3,6,2,4,null,8,1,null,null,null,7,9]`, the LeetCode example).
files.output_note: `chain: 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9`: following only `right` pointers visits the values in sorted order, matching LeetCode's answer. The driver would print `(left child!)` if any node still had a left child; none does.
files.watch_out: Setting `node->left = NULL` is safe only because the left subtree has already been visited before that line.

check.q: What is the dummy node for?
check.a: It gives `current` something to attach the first real node to, so the code needs no special case for the head of the chain.

files.title: LeetCode 1464: maximum product of two elements

problem.name: LeetCode 1464 - Maximum Product of Two Elements in an Array

files.what: Finds the two largest numbers in one pass and returns `(max1 - 1) * (max2 - 1)`.
steps: Keep `max_first` (largest so far) and `max_second` (second largest).
A number bigger than `max_first` pushes the old largest down to `max_second` and takes first place.
Otherwise, if it beats `max_second`, it replaces that.
Return the product of both values minus one.
files.input_note: Number of tests, then for each test n and the n numbers (the two LeetCode examples).
files.output_note: `maxProduct = 12` (4*3 from 5 and 4) and `maxProduct = 16` (4*4 from the two 5s), both as LeetCode expects. The second case shows the `else if` keeps a repeated maximum as the second largest.
files.watch_out: Starting both maxima at 0 works only because the problem guarantees positive values. A max heap (`priority_queue`) popped twice gives the same answer.

check.q: For `[1,5,4,5]`, what are `max_first` and `max_second` at the end?
check.a: Both are 5: the second 5 is not bigger than `max_first` but is bigger than 4, so it becomes `max_second`. The answer is 16.

files.title: Code360: fourth largest element

problem.name: Code360 - Fourth Largest Element In The Array

files.what: Sorts the array in decreasing order and returns the element at index 3, or `INT_MIN` when there are fewer than four elements.
steps: `sort(arr, arr + n, greater<int>())` puts the biggest value first.
The values are copied into `vec_arr`.
If there are fewer than 4 values, return `-2147483648` (the smallest int).
Otherwise return `vec_arr[3]`, the fourth largest.
files.complexity: Time O(n log n) · Space O(n)
files.input_note: Number of tests, then for each test n and the n numbers.
files.output_note: `getFourthLargest = 3`: sorted high to low, the array is 9 6 5 3 1, so index 3 holds 3. The second test has only 3 numbers, so it prints `-2147483648` (INT_MIN), the value the problem asks for when there is no 4th element.
files.watch_out: The file uses `greater<int>` without including `<functional>`. It works on the judge (and here, because the test driver's prelude adds `<bits/stdc++.h>`), but may fail with other compilers. The copy into `vec_arr` is not needed: check `n < 4` and return `arr[3]` directly. A min heap of size 4 would find the answer in O(n log 4).

check.q: How could a min heap of size 4 find the fourth largest value?
check.a: Push each value and pop whenever the size exceeds 4; at the end the heap holds the four largest and its top is the fourth largest.

recap: A heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array: children at `2i+1`, `2i+2`, parent at `(i-1)/2`.
Insert: append, then bubble up while the value beats its parent.
Delete root: move the last value to the top, then push it down towards the better child.
Both heap operations are O(log n).
In-order traversal of a BST gives sorted values; many BST problems build on that.

check_yourself.q: In a heap array, what is the parent index of index 9 and the children of index 4?
check_yourself.a: Parent of 9 is (9 - 1) / 2 = 4. Children of 4 are 9 and 10.

check_yourself.q: Is the array `50 30 40 35 10` a valid max heap?
check_yourself.a: No. Index 3 (value 35) has parent index 1 (value 30), and 35 > 30.

check_yourself.q: Why can't we just delete `v[0]` with `erase` in a heap?
check_yourself.a: Shifting every element left scrambles the parent-child positions, so the heap rule breaks and the cost is O(n). Moving the last element up and pushing it down keeps the shape and costs O(log n).
